analysis.title: Copper November Outlook: Cautious near-term to $13,300/t – Revising our forecasts, balance, plus GCET update
key_insights: Citi cuts its 0-3 month copper price forecast to $13,300/t from $14,500/t, which is also the current 50-day moving average. It expects prices to grind lower over the coming weeks on broad de-risking tied to AI scepticism, weak cyclical demand optimism and a softer 2027 fundamental outlook.
Citi sees consumer dip-buying partly offsetting further selling, given scarce ex-US inventory and ongoing China scrap problems.

Absent a significant tariff announcement, Citi now models a copper surplus on paper for 2027 and 2028 at current prices. Mine supply recovers and AI and energy transition demand growth slows, even with a modest cyclical demand pickup assumed.

Copper faces two-way near-term policy risk from US copper tariff uncertainty and the US-Iran conflict. If further net selling plays out, fund positioning would be cleaner and prices vulnerable to rapid gains if these outcomes turn bullish, or on fresh China stimulus or major supply curtailments.

Net fund positioning has unwound from about 8/10 to about 4/10 (10 = record 2024 peak) on long liquidation against a modest price pullback, with limited fresh short additions. Citi reads this as risk reduction rather than rising bearish conviction.

Scenario weights for the price path: Bull 30%, Base 50%, Bear 20%. Base is $13,500/t for 6-12 months, $13,500/t for 2027 and $14,000/t for 2028. Bull is $16,500/t for 2027 and $18,000/t for 2028. Bear is $12,000/t for 2027 and 2028.

Refined balance: surplus of 257kt in 2026f, 138kt in 2027f and 285kt in 2028f. Mine production growth is 0.7% in 2026f, 2.4% in 2027f and 2.7% in 2028f. Mine supply forecasts were revised higher, including stronger DR Congo growth.

Consumption changes include weaker solar installation expectations for 2026 and 2027. Slowing energy transition and AI growth is offset by a modest cyclical recovery, assuming easing energy prices and sufficient China stimulus. Citi assumes AI datacentre demand flatlines from 2028.

China physical tightness supports dip-buying. SHFE inventory is near multi-year lows and China import premiums over LME are at a multi-year record high. Consumers hold low inventories, so restocking potential is strong on further investor-led price declines.

Citi's Global Copper End-Use Tracker (GCET) shows global implied copper end-use grew about 2.4% y/y in Sep'26. China grew about 2%, mostly from solar (+40% y/y), wind (+128% y/y) and non-renewables (+50% y/y), all from low bases. Excluding solar and wind, China was broadly flat.
Ex-China implied copper end-use grew about 3% y/y in Sep'26, driven by machinery, power grid and generation, and AI datacentre capex. Deteriorating AI sentiment is a downside risk to this.

China's Oct PMI prints returned to contraction, with production and new orders both declining. Ex-China PMIs are in expansion, but the strength comes from AI-linked sectors rather than traditional cyclical sectors, so it is not showing up in cyclical copper use. Citi sees further China policy support as ultimately unavoidable.

About 20% of copper demand comes from energy transition and AI, and has driven close to 100% of demand growth in recent years. Both segments face growth headwinds into 2027, including removal of China export incentives, higher taxes and rising trade barriers. Energy transition spend is about 3x as copper intensive per dollar as datacentre spend.

Scrap supply response is weak. Global secondary refined output grew about 5.4% y/y in Jan-Aug'26 against about 12% implied by historical elasticity at copper prices about 40% higher y/y. Causes include high energy and fuel costs, weaker China trade-in support, a crackdown on provincial subsidies and scrap invoicing, and a depleted scrap chain.

Convenience yields show scarcity of ex-US units. New York is at zero because COMEX spreads trade at full cost of finance on abundant inventory. London spreads are very tight on scarce inventory outside China and the US. Shanghai spreads show an increasingly constrained China inventory environment.

Citi does not expect tariff clarity before 2027, and calls implementation a coin toss. It argues the more the market prices a tariff, the less likely one is near-term, because the status quo keeps metal in the US. The COMEX-LME arb could come under pressure in late December and early January if no tariff news arrives by 1-Jan-27, its base case. A pullback in tariff expectations would likely prompt risk-off behaviour.

Citi does not think the US mid-term election outcome makes tariffs more or less likely. New tariffs would be unfavourable optically after a vote against a high cost of living, and would undermine the tariff support for US semis producers who lobbied for them.

Visible copper inventory builds are about 400kt year to date, including about 600kt in US exchange inventory. The US implied inventory build since March 2025 totals about 1.4Mt, including about 0.4Mt implied shadow stock. Citi attributes the builds to inventory shifting and ex-US destocking as much as to surplus.

Mine supply is near flat in 2026 (+0.7%), returning to trend in 2027 and 2028. Citi assumes a full Grasberg restart by 2028, a late-2027 Cobre Panama restart and resilient DR Congo growth. The disruption allowance is 5.5% in 2027 and 6.6% in 2028, and DR Congo growth is the most uncertain variable.

China EV exports offset weak domestic sales. Domestic plug-in retail sales are down 12% YTD (9M'26), about 1.1mn fewer units. EV exports grew about 140% YTD to about 3.9mn units, and Citi expects above 5.5mn for the year on front-loading ahead of an EU-China cap on PHEV exports of 350k units from early 2027.
China battery output grew about 60% YTD (9M'26), ESS output grew 113% and battery exports grew 52%. ESS is about 45% of battery output.

sector_views.rationale: Citi is cautious near-term with a $13,300/t 0-3 month target, citing AI-driven de-risking, a 2027-28 surplus and sluggish cyclical demand. It also flags upside risk from tariffs, China stimulus and supply disruption.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Well below the ~12% implied by historical scrap elasticity at current copper prices.

risk_factors: Copper fund positioning is sensitive to further equity market pullbacks and AI sentiment deterioration.
Two-way risk from US copper tariff outcomes and the US-Iran conflict.

Mine supply growth in 2027 depends on major restarts and ramp-ups at Grasberg and Cobre Panama and on DR Congo growth, all subject to delay and disruption, and Chile output risks skew to the downside.
DR Congo's rising supply share increases concentration risk.
Supply could surprise to the upside on stronger DR Congo growth, lower disruption or stronger China scrap.
High DM interest rates and China economic headwinds weigh on cyclical demand.

Energy transition copper demand growth may slow in 2027 on removal of China export incentives, higher taxes and trade barriers. AI and datacentre spend crowding out power infrastructure spend would be net bearish for physical copper.
Possible China stimulus, new supply curtailments, inventory hoarding in the US and China, or re-emerging debasement fears could push prices up sharply.

vol_and_positioning: Net fund copper positioning across COMEX and LME fell from about 8/10 to about 4/10 (10 = record 2024 peak) on long liquidation in October, with limited fresh short additions.

Gross fund copper length is well below the 2024 highs in volume terms and, to a lesser extent, in value. As a share of US household financial wealth, room for more allocation versus the 2024 peak is clearer.
Fund positioning is sensitive to further equity pullbacks, such as further AI sentiment deterioration.
COMEX convenience yields are at zero, with spreads at the full cost of finance. London and Shanghai spreads are tight, reflecting scarcity.
The COMEX-LME arb is exposed to fund-led flat price de-risking on AI equity weakness, and to no tariff news by 1-Jan-27.
geopolitical: US-Iran conflict and a possible deal create two-way risk for copper and energy prices.
Strait of Hormuz closure raised fuel costs and so scrap recovery costs.
US Section 232 copper tariff uncertainty and the lack of clarity before 2027.
US-Canada and US-Mexico trade negotiations could be complicated by near-term tariff announcements.
EU-China agreement capping PHEV exports at 350k units from early 2027, and planned reductions in China VAT export rebates.
US mid-term election results removed some uncertainty overhang.

tension_points.bull_case: Physical tightness persists with China scrap problems and depleted ex-US refined inventories. Fund length has already retreated, so a US copper tariff, a conclusive Strait of Hormuz deal, China stimulus or supply curtailments could bring buyers back rapidly. Energy transition and AI are longer-term demand drivers.
tension_points.bear_case: Citi models a 2027 and 2028 surplus at current prices, with stronger mine supply, slowing AI and energy transition demand growth and sluggish cyclical demand under high DM interest rates. Funds remain sensitive to further AI equity weakness.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A significant US copper tariff announcement, or fresh China stimulus or major supply curtailments, would undermine the base case of a grind lower to $13,300/t.

tension_points.bull_case: A US copper tariff announcement would let fund length return rapidly and lift COMEX prices.
tension_points.bear_case: Citi calls implementation a coin toss with no clarity expected before 2027. The more the market prices a tariff, the less likely one is near-term, and a pullback in tariff expectations would likely prompt risk-off behaviour.
tension_points.what_invalidates: No tariff news by 1-Jan-27 is Citi's base case and would pressure the COMEX-LME arb in late December and early January.
